failure_control.evidence: Eight planted controls run on the default path; the run exits nonzero if any is not rejected, and the control COUNT is measured (rejected() records each call; the exit gate compares the number that executed against EXPECTED_CONTROLS and the receipt publishes it), so deleting a control block fails instead of publishing a stale total. The headline control re-creates the external verifier's hardcoded (min_dual=7, rhs=4) logic and hands it the Petersen graph, which that logic calls REFUTED and the computed pipeline clears; a second control plants the literal lambda_min=-4 on the same graph and requires lambda_min_is_derived() -- the gate every published lambda_min passes -- to reject it; a third uses a NON-REGULAR girth-7 graph so the exact Fraction in min_dual_degree() is exercised rather than assumed. Thirteen single-line source mutations, plus one poisoned receipt field, were applied to a clean copy and each was MEASURED to exit 1 (README, 'Measured mutation battery'). BOUNDARY, stated in the verifier and the README: none of this defends against edits to verify.py itself -- a deleted check stays deleted. The exit gate is made tamper-EVIDENT (it recomputes from per-check and per-control records instead of trusting the FAILURES side effect, and cross-checks the two accountings), which is why no-oping that accumulator no longer disarms the controls, but the real defenses against a corrupted verifier are the artifact sha256 pins in this file, the stdout_not_contains '[FAIL]' pin, and git history. Three earlier 'controls' asserting min d* in {6,8,3} were REMOVED, not counted: they compared two already-computed constants and still printed '[ok] rejected' under the min_dual_degree stub this lane exists to catch.
